name: Iterative policy evaluation update

symbols.meaning: new value of s, computed from the old values of its successors

intuition: Use the Bellman equation as an assignment: replace each state's value by the one-step lookahead computed from the current approximation, and repeat.
assumptions: v_0 is arbitrary except that the terminal state, if any, has value 0.
The sequence v_k approaches v_π in the limit whenever v_π itself is guaranteed to exist (γ < 1, or termination from every state).
example: In Example 4.1, one sweep from $v_0 = 0$ gives $v_1(s) = -1$ for every nonterminal state; the second gives $v_2(1) = -1 + \tfrac14(0 - 1 - 1 - 1) = -1.75$.
significance: Each sweep backs up every state once (a full backup). Two arrays implement (4.5) exactly; the in-place variant also converges and usually faster.
pitfalls: Written with v_k on the right, the update is the two-array version; an in-place sweep can use some new values in the same sweep.
Convergence is only in the limit; in practice the loop stops when the largest change falls below θ.

verification.note: The example values are checked by ch04-q002 and ch04.fig4-2-two-array-iterates.

name: Greedy policy improvement

symbols.meaning: value of taking a in s and then following π

intuition: Look one step ahead with $v_\pi$ and pick the action that looks best.
assumptions: Ties may be broken arbitrarily, or shared among the maximizing actions (p. 96).
pitfalls: Improvement needs the model $p(s', r | s, a)$; with only $v_\pi$ and no model it cannot be computed.

name: Value iteration backup

symbols.meaning: the only difference from the policy evaluation backup (4.5)

intuition: One sweep of evaluation with an improvement built in: back up each state with its best action.
assumptions: For arbitrary $v_0$, $v_k \to v_*$ under the conditions that guarantee $v_*$ exists.
pitfalls: Value iteration needs infinitely many sweeps for exact convergence; in practice it stops when the change Δ is small.
